title: Assisted Short Sales for Underwater Auto Loans
one_liner: Record auto originations lead to record delinquencies and a repossession glut. Give lenders a mortgage-style short sale for cars that recovers more than auction does.
customer: Credit unions and subprime and indirect auto lenders with rising 60-plus-day delinquencies.
problem: Auto originations hit a record $211B and auto delinquencies also hit a record (CNBC and others, Aug 2026). Lenders' only tool at scale is repossession and auction, which is slow, costly and yields discounted recoveries. Borrowers keep a deficiency balance and wrecked credit, and lenders lose more than a cooperative sale would cost them.
solution: At 45-60 days delinquent, the lender offers the borrower a lender-blessed voluntary sale. The platform lists the car at retail to dealers and private buyers, handles payoff letters, title and lien release in each state, and converts the shortfall into a small structured note or forgiveness within lender-set limits. The lender pays only when its net recovery beats projected repo loss.
why_now: Delinquencies at records, auction supply pressure, and credit unions with growing delinquent books and a reputation to protect. Mortgage short-sale playbooks are well understood, but nobody has ported them to autos.
revenue_model: Flat fee (about $500-$700) or 3-5% of sale price per completed sale, plus a performance share of recovery improvement over projected repo loss.
non_obvious_insight: Lenders already lose money on repossession, but their servicing, collections and legal workflows are built around it, so no infrastructure exists to choreograph title, payoff and buyer across 50 states. The product is that plumbing.
first_30_days: Partner with two or three credit unions with 5k-plus delinquent auto loans. Run a manual pilot in one state with a small dealer buyer network, comparing net recovery per unit against actual auction results. Use the data to sign a master services agreement.

title: Courthouse Tape: Land-Assembly Radar for Infrastructure
one_liner: A daily feed that reads recorded option memoranda, leases and easements to show who is quietly assembling land for data centers, solar and transmission weeks before anyone announces it.
customer: Competing data center, solar, storage and transmission developers' land teams and site-selection consultants; utility and co-op large-load planners; infrastructure and energy funds buying alternative data; and county economic development and planning offices wanting defensive visibility.
problem: Land assembly is a race, and the first public trace is a short memorandum of option, lease or easement recorded at the county. Nobody watches those at scale. The assessor doesn't reflect an unexercised option. The clerk's document-type field is a dropdown chosen by a data-entry clerk, so big deals hide under 'Other', 'Miscellaneous' or 'Agreement'. Developers find out about a competitor's 6,000 acres months late, counties learn from a leaked newspaper story, and everyone pays landmen $300-$600 a day to sit in vaults.
solution: Ingest recorded instruments from county portals and bulk feeds in target corridors. Classify by reading the full image, not the clerk's label. Cluster by grantee, signatory, notary, return-to law firm and mailing address to unmask LLC families. Flag assembly events, such as N option memos within X miles or easement clusters along a line that imply transmission or pipeline. Deliver alerts, a map, and parcel-level chain-of-title and existing-easement packets on demand, with a human landman reviewing the hard ones.
why_now: The 2025-2026 large-load land rush is real: options in Hallam, Nebraska are reportedly worth tens of thousands of dollars an acre, and Hill County, Texas land appraised near $7,100 an acre has been offered about $100,000 an acre. Options are documented only by memoranda under NDA. FinCEN's 2025 decision to exempt domestic companies from beneficial-ownership reporting means LLC unmasking has to come from primary records. LLM vision finally reads messy scanned instruments accurately.
revenue_model: $2k-$8k/month per regional developer or utility seat, $750-$2,000 per tract title packet, and $50k-$150k/year alt-data licenses for funds. Optional revenue share or free access for counties that provide bulk feeds.
non_obvious_insight: The return-to address and notary on a recorded memorandum are the fingerprint of the developer's counsel, and they reveal an assembly weeks before a rezoning hearing. The mislabeled document-type field is why nobody has done this with generic data vendors. Landmen are the recorder's best regulars and know exactly which counties are hot, which makes them the cheapest ground-truth labelers and first customers.
first_30_days: Choose two counties with a rumored project, pull 24 months of instruments, and build the classifier and clustering. Deliver a 'who is assembling where' memo free to 10 site-selection consultants and land brokers, then convert two into $3k-$5k pilots. Check each state's bulk-data commercial-use rules and offer the counties access to the same maps.

title: Distressed Recycling Equipment Exchange
one_liner: A broker-refurbisher that moves equipment from failed US recycling plants to funded buyers abroad, with commissioning included.
customer: Recyclers in India, Mexico, Turkey, Southeast Asia and Africa building capacity (buyers), sourcing from receivers, lenders and former owners.
problem: More than a quarter of US PET recycling capacity closed in 12 months (7 of about 30). Ascend Elements filed Chapter 11 in April 2026, Li-Cycle went bankrupt in 2025, and Solarcycle paused a plant. Washing lines, extruders, optical sorters and reactors are stranded, while India earmarked about $166M to subsidize recycling capacity.
solution: Catalog equipment with photos and condition reports, bundle it into 'line packages', refurbish and test, ship, and send a commissioning team. Give buyers financing-ready documentation and give receivers a fast, credible exit.
why_now: 2025-26 produced an unusual wave of high-spec recycling plant failures, and subsidy money abroad creates buyers, both at once.
revenue_model: 10-20% commission on sales plus refurbishment and commissioning fees.
non_obvious_insight: General industrial liquidators do not know which line is a working PET wash line. Domain knowledge plus buyer matching is the margin, and it grows every time another recycler fails.
first_30_days: Contact the receivers and lenders for the 7 closed reclaimers and other failed plants. Build an equipment inventory with photos. Pre-sell to 5 Indian or Mexican buyers before taking on any inventory.

title: Work-Authorization Continuity Benefit for Care Employers
one_liner: An employer-paid benefit that screens every care worker for legal pathways, tracks EAD renewals and reverification, and plans backfill.
customer: Home-care agencies, nursing homes and assisted-living groups with 50-2,000 workers, especially in NY, FL, MA, MN, WI and CA, and staffing agencies.
problem: 30% of direct care workers are immigrants (60% in New York), and about 350,000 Haitians lost TPS on Aug 4. At least one in five immigrant direct-care workers come from countries hit by the 75-country visa pause. With turnover already at 77-80%, losing staff means closed beds, and few workers have been screened for family, asylum, adjustment or other pathways.
solution: A per-worker monthly benefit: confidential attorney-led status screening and pathway triage, EAD and renewal tracking with on-time filing, an I-9 reverification calendar with non-discriminatory templates, workforce-at-risk forecasting by site and date, and fast backfill through a partner training school. Employers see aggregate risk, not individual status.
why_now: The 2026 visa pause, TPS terminations and a DOL proposal to roll back home-care wage protections hit at once, and Wisconsin agencies say they're 'just not able to take new clients.' Employers need something other than lobbying.
revenue_model: $8-15 per worker per month (employer-paid), plus filing fees with 20-30% margin and optional filing-fee financing.
non_obvious_insight: Immigration compliance is treated as static HR paperwork, but for care employers it is now a retention and continuity problem. Attorney-led screening can surface pathways that keep workers, which is worth thousands per retained caregiver.
first_30_days: Partner with an immigration law firm and a Haitian community organization, sign three agencies with Haitian-heavy workforces (NY, FL, MA), and pilot with 200 workers.

title: Retreat Options for Eroding Oceanfront Homes
one_liner: An annual retainer that reserves a house-mover and demolition slot and triggers automatically when satellite-measured setback hits a preset distance.
customer: Owners of oceanfront and bluff homes on the Outer Banks and Cape Hatteras, Great Lakes bluffs, Maine and Nantucket, and California bluffs. Secondary buyers are lenders, county governments and the National Park Service.
problem: 32 oceanfront houses have collapsed along Cape Hatteras National Seashore since 2020, four in one February 2026 weekend. Owners bear removal costs of roughly $120K to demolish or $100K-$200K to move. NFIP pays nothing pre-collapse, and contractor capacity is overwhelmed exactly when it is needed. NFIP pre-collapse coverage has been proposed but not enacted.
solution: Pooled owners pay a retainer for two things. First, monthly satellite measurement of foundation-to-scarp or vegetation-line distance from 30-50 cm imagery, with pre-storm tasking, and archive imagery to compute each home's 5-10 year retreat rate. Second, pre-negotiated capacity with movers and demolition contractors. Preset thresholds automatically mobilise the contractor and deliver a dated evidence file. That file doubles as claim documentation if NFIP pre-collapse legislation passes and gives lenders and counties a trusted trigger. Structured as a service and capacity contract rather than insurance.
why_now: FEMA's lack of any pre-collapse option is national news in September 2026 (NPR), and the Outer Banks lost 20 Buxton houses in a year. Pre-collapse coverage legislation is pending. Cheap oversupplied commercial imagery makes pooled tasking affordable (one 25 km2 pass covers about 10 km of coast and hundreds of homes).
revenue_model: $1,800/yr retainer per home. An 8-10% referral fee on move or demolition jobs. County and NPS triage contracts. Lender monitoring feeds at $10-20 per loan per month.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce resource is neither money nor measurement but contractor capacity at the moment of crisis. An option on that capacity, triggered by a measurement all parties trust, is a new kind of asset. Neighbours pooling their tasking makes the satellite cost trivial per home.
first_30_days: Sign 2 Outer Banks or Great Lakes house-movers and demolition firms to retainer terms. Pull archive imagery to compute 5-year retreat rates for about 200 threatened homes, then approach owner associations in Buxton and Rodanthe with each home's own curve. Enrol 10 homes at $1,200 founder pricing.

title: Youth Clubs as the Ban-Proof Group Chat
one_liner: A roster-anchored messaging layer for sports leagues, scout councils and youth groups that reuses the club's adult-verified roster as a safe, auditable chat for 9-15 year olds, paid by the club.
customer: Regional youth sports leagues, scout councils, robotics/FIRST teams and church youth groups (5k-100k members), plus their liability insurers. Parents use it free.
problem: Under-16 bans (Australia, Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, several US states) push kids into private chats and games. Everyone's answer is a new 'safe social network for kids', which dies on cold start. Meanwhile clubs already hold the verified network (background-checked coaches, rosters, parent contacts) but run it on WhatsApp, GroupMe and Snap groups with coach-to-child DMs. Youth-safety policies such as SafeSport's (from memory) prohibit exactly those DMs, and leagues cannot audit them.
solution: Team and league chats built on the registration data the club already has (DOB, parent identity). No one-to-one adult-minor DMs unless a second guardian is copied. Kid accounts are age-tiered and parent-linked, with no discovery, ads or strangers. Keyword flags go to the club safety officer. An exportable audit log goes to the insurer. Kids age out into open platforms at 16.
why_now: Ban leakage (VPNs under A$20 a month, 75% of Australian teens planning to stay on) means kids need somewhere else to talk. Insurers are tightening abuse-and-molestation coverage (from memory). Fall registration season is happening now, so the product can ride the season's registration fee.
revenue_model: $1-4 per member per season, bundled into the league's registration fee. Enterprise licence for councils. Referral fees or premium credits from insurers.
non_obvious_insight: The hard part of safe kids' social is distribution and verification, not software. A club has the graph, the identity check, a legal duty of care and a budget, and nobody has packaged that.
first_30_days: Interview 15 league directors and two youth-sports insurers. Ship a white-label chat on Stream or Sendbird for two leagues in one metro. Sell it as 'audit-ready coach-athlete messaging' at $1 per kid during fall registration. Collect an insurer endorsement or premium-credit letter.

title: Fandom Events in Empty Cinema Auditoriums
one_liner: A rights-plus-ticketing agency that fills weekday auditoriums with VTuber concert viewings, esports finals and game-reveal nights, splitting the box office with cinema chains.
customer: Fandom promoters and community organizers, VTuber agencies, esports and game publishers wanting fan events, and regional cinema chains as venue partners. Fans pay $15-30.
problem: Overseas viewers are about 30% of Hololive viewership and roughly 10B yen of revenue, yet have no communal way to attend, while Sphere-scale venues cost hundreds of millions and Live Nation controls arenas. Independent organizers rent bars with poor AV and no rights.
solution: Package a dark room, great sound and a projection booth with the rest of the event: sublicensed rights, a licensed live feed, all-in-price ticketing, cosplay contests and merch tables. Start with regional independent chains and a fixed menu of event formats.
why_now: Hololive concert revenue grew 18.7% and overseas fandom is underserved. The FTC's all-in-pricing rule and the Live Nation verdict make promoters and fans look for alternatives to arena ticketing. Cinemas still need non-Hollywood content for off-peak seats.
revenue_model: 15-25% of ticket revenue plus $2-8k per event for rights and technical fees, with cinemas taking a box-office split and concessions.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce ingredient in experience-economy fandom is not a $2B dome, it's a room with audio and projection, which cinemas already own and leave empty midweek. Everyone is chasing IP-in-space capex while the arbitrage is empty seats.
first_30_days: Pitch 5 independent cinema owners on a revenue split. Sign one rights-cleared event, such as a fighting-game grand finals viewing or a licensed VTuber concert screening. Run three test events by day 45 and measure fill rate and concession spend.

title: Satellite Settlement Radar for Condo Buildings
one_liner: Use free satellite radar archives to give condo boards a 10-year movement history of their building, and turn it into litigation-grade evidence when a neighboring construction project caused the settlement.
customer: Florida condo associations and property managers (3+ story buildings under post-Surfside milestone and reserve-study rules), structural engineers doing milestone inspections (white-label), buyers' agents, lenders and insurers.
problem: Milestone inspections and reserve studies are snapshots, while settlement is a trend. Boards face assessments of $30k to $100k+ per unit and don't know whether nearby construction is moving their building. A University of Miami-led study of Sentinel-1 data found subsidence of up to 8 cm in the Sunny Isles and Surfside area between 2016 and 2023 and linked it to nearby construction, yet no local product turns that into building-level reports for boards.
solution: A six-page Settlement Screening Report per building. Run open-source InSAR pipelines on Sentinel-1 (and newer radar sources) for large-footprint or tall buildings, overlay neighboring construction permits and pile-driving dates, and flag movement trends and differential settlement. Engineers can rely on it as a screening input. Optional monthly monitoring, and a litigation package with a geodesy expert declaration for claims against adjacent developers.
why_now: Post-Surfside laws now force inspections and funded reserves, so boards are spending on engineers. Free multi-year radar archives and mature open-source processing (ASF HyP3, MintPy) mean a two-person team can process buildings retroactively. Incumbents (engineers, inspectors, insurers) have not integrated satellite evidence.
revenue_model: $750 to $2,500 per building per year, $300 wholesale per building for engineering partners, monitoring subscriptions, and contingency or expert fees on construction-damage claims.
non_obvious_insight: The archive already recorded the history, so on day one you can hand a board a decade of movement. The money is in the claim, not the report: construction-induced settlement is an insurable, litigable harm, and radar time series with permit overlays date the cause. Sell the report as the intake funnel for claim work with construction-defect counsel.
first_30_days: Process 50 buildings along the Miami Beach to Sunny Isles corridor with open tools and publish a free hotspot map. Contact 100 condo boards and 10 structural engineering firms. Sell five reports at $750 and sign one construction-defect litigator as a partner. Note the limits (resolution favors large buildings) in every report.

title: Thermal Safety Certification for Recovery Studios
one_liner: Staff certification, medication-aware intake screening and water-quality logging that insurers will soon require of sauna and cold-plunge operators.
customer: Contrast-therapy studios, gym recovery rooms, hotels and spas, paying monthly per location.
problem: Chain: studios are rolling out at speed (one brand added 25 locations in about 20 months and plans 100 more), so hundreds of new hires with no clinical training run 190F rooms and shared 40F tubs; customers increasingly take GLP-1s, blood-pressure meds or diuretics that raise fainting and dehydration risk; shared plunge water has no consistent standard and health departments are unsure how to classify it. One serious incident will trigger insurer exclusions and regulator attention.
solution: Three-part kit: a 90-minute 'Thermal Host' certification with annual refresh; tablet check-in screening (conditions and medications mapped to green/yellow/red session guidance plus waiver logging); and a water sensor pack (ORP, pH, chlorine, temperature) that auto-generates logs for inspectors and insurers.
why_now: The recovery boom (Nordic-style attendance up about 33 percent in 2025), mass GLP-1 use (about 1 in 8 adults), and no existing standard mean insurers and health departments are about to look for controls.
revenue_model: $99-199 per month per location, $39 per staff certification, sensor rental $49 per month per tub, plus insurer or broker referral fees.
non_obvious_insight: Be the standard before the incident: insurers would rather subsidize a certification than write exclusions, and the screening data is a wedge to premium programs. GLP-1 plus heat is the specific collision no one is training for.
first_30_days: Draft the protocol with a sports-medicine physician and a pool-operations consultant, sell it to 5 independent studios in one metro at a discounted founding rate, and ask two studio-focused insurance brokers for a premium credit for certified locations.

title: Driver's Ed for Smartphones, Sold to Parent Groups
one_liner: Ten-week, cohort-based 'phone license' programs where a whole grade's parents and kids pledge together, kids earn tiered device access through in-person challenges, and the finish is a coming-of-age ceremony.
customer: Parent groups for one grade at one school (PTA/PTO, church youth groups, scout troops, neighborhoods) with kids aged 9-13 facing the first-smartphone decision. Parents pay about $249 per child. PTAs get a rev-share. Later: device partners and employers offering parent benefits.
problem: The first smartphone is a collective-action problem ('everyone else has one'). Parental-control software fails technically (7 in 10 Australian under-16s reportedly still hold accounts) and socially. The first phone has become an unguided adolescent initiation with no ritual, no community and no meaning, while loneliness among the young is rising.
solution: 1) A Parent Pact night to agree shared rules. 2) Ten weekly 90-minute kid sessions with trained youth facilitators covering boredom, friendship, spotting manipulative design, AI-companion literacy and group-chat etiquette, with badges earned in person. 3) Tiered device 'licenses': none, then dumbphone or watch, then a filtered smartphone using OS-level age signals, then full access, each unlocked at cohort milestones with parent sign-off. 4) A License Ceremony with families. 5) An alumni circle with monthly meetups and a parent forum.
why_now: Under-16 bans (Australia Dec 2025, Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Florida) and app-store or OS-level age-assurance laws (California's Digital Age Assurance Act, Texas) are tiering the internet by age. Roblox now tiers by age (Kids, Select, standard). Support for Australia's ban has fallen to 57% and enforcement is leaky, so parents need a home-side complement. Twelve US states have school phone bans.
revenue_model: About $249 per child per cohort, a 15% rev-share to PTAs, bounties on tier-appropriate device or plan activations (verify what partners will pay), a $600 facilitator certification for teachers and youth workers, and later employer-paid parent benefits.
non_obvious_insight: The first smartphone fails as a family decision but works as a class decision. Because the product synchronizes a social graph, its moat is the cohort, not code. And a secular rite of passage supplies the 'meaning' that makes kids willing, which content-filtering apps cannot provide.
first_30_days: Pilot with two elementary schools' 4th- and 5th-grade parent groups through PTA presidents and 'Wait Until 8th' pledge lists. Recruit four facilitators (education or psychology students and retired coaches). Charge $249, run cohorts October-December so graduation lands before holiday phone gifting, and track how many kids stay phone-free until 13.

title: Contingency-Fee 45F Childcare Tax Credit Shop
one_liner: An R&D-credit-style boutique that finds, structures and files the newly expanded employer childcare credit (40%, or 50% for small businesses, capped at $500k/$600k) for firms already spending on childcare.
customer: Mid-market employers (200-5,000 staff) with onsite care or vendor childcare spend: hospitals, manufacturers, universities, credit unions and restaurant chains. Referral channel: their CPA firms.
problem: The 45F credit was rarely used under its old cap. From January 1, 2026 the credit rose to 40% (50% small business) with $500k ($600k) caps. Eligibility turns on contract structure, licensing, enrollment open to employees and documentation, and it interacts with the new $7,500 DCFSA limit. Generalist CPAs don't know it and CFOs have never claimed it.
solution: A two-week diagnostic reviews contracts and spend, restructures where needed (for example, reserved-slot agreements with licensed local centers or consortium models), computes the credit and files the forms alongside the client's CPA. Reserved-slot deals also give centers guaranteed enrollment, which helps supply.
why_now: The changes took effect January 2026, employers set 2027 benefit budgets in Q4 2026, and the first full filing season under the new rules is early 2027.
revenue_model: Contingency fee of 15-20% of credit claimed (a $250k credit yields $40-50k). Add-on brokerage fee for slot-reservation contracts.
non_obvious_insight: A $500k cap means the credit can fund a whole classroom's worth of care per employer. The constraint is know-how, not money, and reserved-slot contracts turn a tax credit into childcare supply, a desert fix hidden in the tax code.
first_30_days: Partner with a tax attorney or CPA who has done R&D or WOTC credits. Build a list of 200 employers advertising childcare benefits (job posts, hospital filings). Publish a two-page 45F guide and a free eligibility screen. Aim for 3 signed contingency engagements.

title: Repair-Rights Compliance Portal in a Box
one_liner: A hosted repair.yourbrand.com that publishes the parts lists, manuals, pricing and order forms that US state and EU repair laws require, plus the rules engine and audit trail behind it.
customer: Compliance, legal and customer-service leads at mid-market consumer-electronics, appliance, e-bike, power-tool and mobility brands ($30M-$1B revenue) selling in Washington, Texas, Oregon and the EU. Retailers are a second segment.
problem: Washington's law took effect 1 Jan 2026, Texas applies from Sep 2026 to electronics over $50, Oregon bans parts pairing, the EU directive's transposition deadline was 31 Jul 2026, and an EU repair platform is due 1 Jan 2028. Each regime differs in scope, dates and price rules, and the briefing found nobody selling compliance tooling for repair-information forms or parts-availability tracking.
solution: Portal templates and connectors: product-catalog import, SKU mapping to state or EU scope and effective dates, auto-published manuals and parts lists, a parts order form with a fair-price check, pairing-policy disclosures, an SLA timer and request log for regulators, and an EU repair-information-form generator. Regulatory updates ship as configuration changes.
why_now: Multiple obligations hit in the past nine months (Washington Jan 2026, EU transposition Jul 2026, Texas Sep 2026) and Oregon dates are still unclear in public sources, so brands cannot rely on a single law-firm memo.
revenue_model: $15-60k/year per brand by SKU count, $10-30k implementation, and a per-order fee on parts sales.
non_obvious_insight: The core burden of repair law is publication and response time, which is CMS and workflow work, not legal analysis. Law firms bill hourly for what is really a web app, and the portal also cuts support costs.
first_30_days: Pick 30 mid-market brands with Texas exposure from product listings and email compliance leads a free one-page 'Texas gap audit'. Build a minimal portal for three design partners at a $5k pilot fee.

title: Vacant-House Concierge for Parents Moving Into Care
one_liner: One monthly plan that insures, inspects, maintains and eventually sells the house left empty when a parent moves to memory care or dies.
customer: Adult children and executors (45-65), often out of state, acting under POA or as executor. The channels are elder-law and estate attorneys, memory-care sales directors and senior move managers.
problem: When a parent moves into care, the house sits empty for 3-12 months. Homeowners policies typically restrict coverage after 30-60 days of vacancy, and pipes, taxes, utilities, break-ins and mail scams pile up. Probate cases rose about 32% from 2020 to 2024, and exhausted heirs are unprepared.
solution: A $199-449 monthly plan: vacancy-compliant insurance via an MGA partner, weekly inspections with water, temperature and entry sensors, autopay of utilities, taxes and HOA from an estate or POA account, seasonal maintenance, mail forwarding, sibling portal, documentation for the estate accounting, then cleanout, staging and a sell-when-ready referral.
why_now: The 80+ cohort is growing about 36.6% over the decade, senior housing is at 90% occupancy so moves happen in crises, and the $6T wealth transfer is underway. Heirs are far-flung Gen X executors who need a service, not a checklist.
revenue_model: Monthly subscription, insurance commissions, cleanout and staging fees, and a referral or flat fee on the eventual sale.
non_obvious_insight: Estate-settlement startups start at death, but the costly, uninsured window opens at the care move, years earlier. Anchoring on that moment gives access to the family before competitors and before the house loses value.
first_30_days: In one metro dense with senior housing, recruit 10 estate and elder-law attorneys and five move managers, secure a vacancy-insurance MGA quote, and sign the first 10 homes at an introductory rate.

title: Foreign-Ties Clearance Pack for SBIR Startups
one_liner: A fixed-price, agency-ready foreign-involvement and cyber-readiness dossier priced to fit inside the SBIR technical-assistance allowance, so the startup pays nothing out of pocket.
customer: SBIR/STTR Phase I and Phase II applicants and awardees (DoD, DOE, NSF, NIH, EPA). Secondary buyers are seed and VC funds with SBIR-heavy portfolios that need LP-level attestations for their companies.
problem: The Small Business Innovation and Economic Security Act (S. 3971, signed April 13, 2026, extends SBIR/STTR through FY2031) makes agencies run risk-based due diligence on every applicant. The review covers foreign ownership and financial ties, foreign affiliations of key personnel, licensing deals and joint ventures, and links to the UFLPA, Chinese Military-Industrial Complex, Commerce Entity and Section 889 lists. It also covers cybersecurity practices, patent analysis and employee analysis. Applicants must file disclosures. A 4-person startup has no idea what an agency will find in its cap table (LPs behind the VC funds), co-inventors, or contractors. Agencies may notify of a denial only 'as appropriate', so a rejection may come with no explanation.
solution: A software-plus-analyst service that ingests the cap table, team list, patents and vendor list. It does look-through on investors (SEC Form ADV and Form D, GLEIF, OpenCorporates). It screens every name against the free BIS Consolidated Screening List and the UFLPA and CMIC lists. It checks co-inventor and employee affiliations (USPTO PatentsView, ORCID) and takes a NIST 800-171/SPRS cyber baseline. Output is a disclosure-ready packet, a red-flag remediation memo (for example 'restructure this side letter'), and a yearly re-screen. Sold as a vendor the awardee can pick for technical and business assistance (T&BA) money.
why_now: S. 3971 was signed April 13, 2026. The T&BA allowance was raised to $6,500 per Phase I and $50,000 per Phase II, and it now explicitly covers 'cybersecurity assistance' and 'screening for potential foreign involvement'. The lapse from October 2025 to April 2026 created a backlog: DOE alone opened about $147M of FY25 Phase II on July 22, 2026, and the FY26 Genesis Mission Phase I is open. Every awardee now faces the new diligence for the first time.
revenue_model: $2,500 to $6,500 flat per Phase I (fits under the $6,500 T&BA cap, so it is free to the founder). $15k to $50k per Phase II package. $1,200 per year for a re-screen subscription when the cap table changes. VC portfolio bundles at $500 to $1,000 per company.
non_obvious_insight: Congress created an earmarked wallet for exactly this service, and the buyer has zero price sensitivity because the money can't be spent on anything else. S. 3971 Section 7 amends Section 9(q) to allow T&BA funds for 'cybersecurity assistance' and 'screening for potential foreign involvement', up to $6,500 (Phase I) and $50,000 (Phase II) per project, and lets recipients choose their own vendors. Section 2 (new Section 9(vv)) lists the diligence factors agencies must assess (https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/BILLS-119s3971enr/html/BILLS-119s3971enr.htm). DOE confirms the April 13, 2026 signing, extension through FY2031, new security due-diligence mandates, and the reopened Phase II money (https://www.energy.gov/technologycommercialization/doe-small-business-innovation-research-sbir-and-small-business). The hard part is not screening names but LP-level look-through on venture funds, which is opaque and which no compliance vendor packages for a 4-person startup. Caveat: I could not confirm which agencies have opened T&BA vendor lists yet, so check that first.
first_30_days: Week 1: build a free 'SBIR foreign-risk self-check' web tool on top of the BIS Consolidated Screening List API and the UFLPA list. Use it as the lead magnet. Weeks 1 to 2: pull the last 12 months of Phase I/II awardees from the public SBIR.gov awards data and email 300 founders quoting the exact statute language. Weeks 2 to 4: manually produce 5 free dossiers for design partners to learn where the LP look-through breaks. Ask each agency SBIR office (start with DOE OTC, NSF and Navy) how to be listed as a T&BA vendor. Close 5 paid packs at $2.5k to $6.5k.

title: Chosen-Kin Circles for Solo Agers
one_liner: Mutual health-care-proxy circles of 3-4 unrelated solo agers with legal packets and a professional backstop, sold as estate planning but delivering belonging.
customer: Adults 55-75 with no spouse or nearby children ($1,200 setup plus $29 a month), referred by elder-law and estate attorneys, and later employers' pre-retirement benefits and health systems.
problem: Trend chain: fewer children and more one-person households (29% of US households), then the first large kinless retirement cohort (roughly one in five older adults is an 'elder orphan' or at risk of becoming one), then hospitals default to statutory next of kin who may not exist or be estranged, ethics reviews and expensive guardianships follow, and nobody shows up. Loneliness and a legal vacuum arrive together.
solution: Match 3-4 members by neighborhood and temperament. Each signs reciprocal state-specific health-care proxy, HIPAA release, POA, pet-care and funeral-wishes documents. The circle meets quarterly at a facilitated dinner to refresh documents and check in. A professional fiduciary is the backstop, and a 24/7 dispatcher runs the call tree when a member is hospitalized, with a wallet card and QR link hospitals can scan.
why_now: The 2024-27 'Peak 65' wave brings about 4 million Americans a year into retirement, including the largest kinless cohort yet. LLM-assisted drafting made state-specific legal packets cheap. Loneliness is now a WHO-measured health metric, so systems are receptive.
revenue_model: Setup fee plus subscription, referral fees from attorneys, and enterprise deals where hospitals or plans pay to reduce unrepresented-patient cases.
non_obvious_insight: People will not pay for friends but will pay for a health-care proxy. Sell the legal and logistics wrapper and let belonging be the by-product. The documents make the circle real, because someone has promised to show up.
first_30_days: Partner with two estate-planning attorneys in one metro. Host three 'Circle Nights' at $299 per person including the document packet, and capture 30 members. Contract a fiduciary for the backstop.

title: Pharmacy Friendly Calls, Paid by Adherence Stars
one_liner: Independent pharmacies run weekly human-led friendship calls to isolated refill customers, funded by the Medicare adherence performance that loneliness quietly erodes.
customer: Independent community pharmacies (roughly 18,000 in the US) paying $500-1,200 a month per store, later reimbursed through Medicare Advantage and Part D plan performance and MTM contracts.
problem: Isolated older adults skip refills. Adherence measures for diabetes, RAS-antagonist and statin drugs carry triple weight in Medicare Star ratings, so plans pay for every point. Older adults distrust AI companions (Pew, Jun 2026: 40-46% of 65+ are 'unsure' whether chatbots help or hurt), and startup elder-companion services lack a trusted local face. The corner pharmacist has that trust and a list of exactly who is isolated.
solution: A 'Pharmacy Pal' program. Each store enrolls 40-80 living-alone or homebound refill customers. A paid part-time caller (a retiree or pharmacy tech) makes a weekly 10-minute call using an AI-prepared brief (last call notes, refill gaps, birthdays), and also does a twice-monthly delivery run. Software covers rosters, call briefs, refill-gap alerts and a proportion-of-days-covered dashboard the pharmacy can show plans. The AI never talks to the patient.
why_now: Chain-store closures (Rite Aid's 2025 wind-down among them) made independents the last local pharmacy for many seniors. Plans are squeezed on Star bonuses and margins and want cheap, measurable adherence levers. Pew's 2026 data show older adults distrust chatbots, which reopens the case for human-led programs.
revenue_model: $12-18 per enrolled patient per month, paid by the pharmacy out of retained refills, delivery fees and plan MTM or performance-network payments. Phase two is direct plan contracts priced on measured adherence lift.
non_obvious_insight: Insiders look for an elder-companion buyer among families and social-service agencies. The real loneliness budget for older adults sits inside Star-rating adherence economics, and the trusted delivery channel is the local pharmacist, not an app.
first_30_days: Recruit 5 independent pharmacies through state pharmacist associations and PSAO newsletters. Each pulls 40 patients from refill-gap reports. Run the calls manually with a spreadsheet and an LLM-generated brief. Measure adherence lift against matched non-enrolled patients over 90 days. Charge $500 a month per store from the start.

title: Contingency Audit of Unbilled Plumbing Materials
one_liner: Reconcile a trade shop's supply-house invoices against its customer invoices and catch both parts that were bought but never billed and quiet supplier price drift, paid a percentage of what gets recovered.
customer: Plumbing, HVAC and electrical shops doing $1.5-15M in revenue with 5-40 techs, running ServiceTitan, Housecall Pro or Jobber plus QuickBooks, buying on account from Ferguson, Hajoca, Winsupply or a local supply house.
problem: Shops lose margin in two places nobody watches. First, parts go out on a supply-house ticket with a job name, or come off the truck stock, and never make it onto the customer invoice. Techs charge the labor from the flat-rate book and forget the $6 valve, the wax ring, the supply lines, the $40 of fittings. In the shops I know, when the office finally reconciles a quarter it is typically a few percent of revenue. Second, supply houses price off list with a contractor multiplier, and list prices have moved several times since the Section 232 copper, steel and aluminum tariffs (50%, working through a long manufacturer-to-contractor lag). Surcharges appear, job-quoted prices are not honored, returns credits are never issued, and no owner has time to read 40 invoices a week.
solution: Shops set up an email forwarding rule for supply-house invoices and statements and give us read access to their field-service software export. An LLM-based line-item parser ties supply-house lines to jobs and POs, then produces a weekly leak list for the office manager: (1) purchased-not-billed by job, (2) price versus the shop's own multiplier and versus the same SKU 30 days ago, (3) unclaimed return credits, (4) pricebook items where cost has risen past the target markup, with a repricing file ready to import. Later add a benchmark ('you pay 9% more than shops your size for PEX-A fittings') built from pooled anonymized invoices, which is the moat.
why_now: Tariff-driven price volatility means flat-rate pricebooks are stale within a quarter, and owners know it. Invoice parsing with LLMs went from a custom-ML project to an afternoon. Field-service platforms expose APIs and exports. The trades are also ahead of everyone else in adopting software but behind in auditing it, so there is no incumbent audit product.
revenue_model: Contingency fee of 25% of recovered and newly captured revenue for the first 12 months (no recovery, no fee), converting to a $199-499 per month subscription for continuous monitoring plus the pricing benchmark. Data licensing of the pooled price index to distributors and manufacturers later.
non_obvious_insight: Owners obsess over lead cost and tech hiring while the highest-ROI dollar is sitting in the shoebox of paid invoices. Everything a tech installs was bought on a ticket with a job name on it, so the truth is already in two systems that have never been compared. This is the freight-audit and telecom-audit model, and no one has brought it to the trades because the people who feel the pain are too busy running trucks to build it.
first_30_days: Offer a free 90-day audit to 10 shop owners from a peer group (a PHCC chapter, Nexstar or Service Roundtable style mastermind). Have them forward statements and give a one-time export. Turn each audit around in 48 hours with a single 'found money' number and a list of specific invoices. Convert the shops with the largest number to the contingency contract. A spreadsheet plus an LLM parsing script is enough for the first ten.

title: Independent Leakage Audits for Age Verification
one_liner: A red-team lab that measures how easily under-16s slip past each platform's age check (VPN, borrowed ID, face tricks) and sells defensible evidence to platforms, counsel and insurers.
customer: Mid-size social, gaming and video platforms operating in Australia, the UK, Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia and US ban states. Also their outside counsel and, later, regulators.
problem: Insiders treat age assurance as a vendor-selection problem. Regulators judge whether 'reasonable steps' were taken. Australia is investigating five major platforms (fines up to A$49.5M) and proposed in June 2026 to double fines to about A$99M and reach app stores and age-assurance providers. By February 2026 many children had already bypassed the ban. Vendors self-report accuracy but nobody independently measures real-world leakage at the 14-17 border.
solution: A standard test harness of about 20 evasion scenarios (VPN region switch, parent's ID, older-sibling account, face-estimation edge cases, re-registration). It runs with consented adult testers and synthetic profiles, never with minors. Outputs are a quarterly public 'Leakage Index' plus confidential 'reasonable-steps evidence packs' and a continuous monitoring subscription.
why_now: Bans went live between December 2025 and June 2026 and enforcement is starting. The proposed extension of liability to age-assurance providers means everyone in the chain wants third-party evidence. The reported IDScan breach and Persona complaints (both from the brief, one flagged shaky) push platforms to question their vendors.
revenue_model: Confidential audits at $15-60k each. Monitoring subscription at $3-10k a month. Later, licensing the test protocol to regulators and insurers.
non_obvious_insight: This is an assurance market like SOC 2, not a technology market. The buyer wants a defensible paper trail, and it must be independent of the vendors it grades, so the lab should be paid by the platforms rather than the vendors.
first_30_days: Write the 20-scenario protocol with a regulatory lawyer. Run it on 5 public age gates in Australia using adult test accounts, keeping to what counsel clears. Publish a free 'Leakage Index' teaser. Cold-email trust-and-safety leads and regulatory counsel at 40 mid-size platforms with their own results.

title: Data Act Broker for Equipment Owners
one_liner: File and operationalize EU Data Act data-access demands so independent service shops can finally read the diagnostics that elevator, heat-pump, forklift and tractor makers lock away.
customer: Independent maintenance and service companies in the EU (starting with elevator/escalator maintainers, then commercial heat-pump installers, forklift and ag-machinery shops). They pay per monitored asset per month. Equipment-owning businesses (building managers, hospitals, logistics sites) are the secondary payer, because they hold the legal right.
problem: Original manufacturers use exclusive access to machine diagnostics and fault logs to keep 60-80% of the lucrative service market. Independents work blind, so they lose contracts to OEMs. The EU Data Act (applicable since 12 Sep 2025) gives the user of a connected product, including a business, the right to get the data the product generates. The user can also have it handed to any third party of their choice. In practice almost nobody exercises the right. The paperwork is unfamiliar, OEMs stall, and the data arrives in a different format from every vendor.
solution: An agency-plus-plumbing service. (1) Sign a user-authorization letter with the equipment owner. (2) Auto-generate and file the Article 4/5 access and third-party-sharing requests to each OEM and track statutory response deadlines. (3) Ingest whatever comes back, whether an API, a file dump or a portal export. (4) Normalize it into one cross-vendor schema per asset class. (5) Give the independent shop a fleet-health dashboard and fault-prediction alerts. Add a public compliance scorecard showing which OEMs comply, and escalate the ones that do not to national enforcement authorities.
why_now: The Data Act became applicable on 12 Sep 2025. On 12 Sep 2026, 16 days ago, its design obligation started applying to newly placed connected products, so data must be accessible by default. The right-to-repair movement is at peak momentum. OEM stonewalling now generates complaints that regulators must act on. No one has industrialized user-side requests yet, so the first mover sets the standard schema and templates.
revenue_model: Setup fee of about 50-150 EUR per asset for the request and integration work, plus 4-12 EUR per asset per month for the normalized feed and health analytics. Add-ons: predictive-maintenance alerts and a white-label owner portal. Later: sell anonymized cross-fleet reliability benchmarks to insurers and asset owners.
non_obvious_insight: A legal right is worthless until someone industrializes exercising it. The Data Act gives the data-access key to the owner, not the repairer, so the winning business acts as the owner's agent and sells the result to the repairer. The moat is accumulated request templates, OEM-by-OEM response knowledge, and one normalized schema. Every OEM refusal also becomes evidence for regulators, which turns compliance friction into marketing.
first_30_days: Pick one vertical and one country pair, for example independent elevator maintainers in Germany and the Netherlands, and reach them through trade associations. Retain a Data Act lawyer for a fixed fee to finalize request templates. Recruit 5 independent shops, get user-authorization letters covering about 50 units, and file the requests. Log every OEM response and format. Charge a pilot fee of about 1-2k EUR per shop for delivered data plus a first fleet report. Publish an OEM response-time tracker to build inbound demand. Expect uneven enforcement, so keep the pilot to OEMs that respond and use the ones that stonewall as regulator evidence.

title: Unwind Desk for California's 3-Day Car Return
one_liner: A per-return concierge that unwinds a cancelled used-car deal (lender, add-on administrators, DMV, sales tax, commissions) inside California's new 48-hour refund deadline. It then turns the return data into a return-risk pool.
customer: California used-car dealers, especially independents and BHPH lots that sell 30 to 200 used cars a month and have no back-office bench. They pay $195 to $250 per return, or a standby retainer. Later, insurers and MGAs buy the underwriting data.
problem: From Oct 1, 2026, SB 766 gives buyers a 3-day right to cancel a used vehicle priced at $50,000 or less. Within 48 hours of cancellation the dealer must cancel the contract and refund the buyer, less only the deductions the law allows for mileage and damage. That is easy to write and very hard to do. The cost of an unwind is the cascade, not the car. The dealer has to reach the lender that has funded or is holding the contract, cancel each service contract and GAP with its administrator, and charge back the F&I commission. It also has to reverse the title, registration and sales tax, refund the down payment and any trade, and document the vehicle condition to justify any deduction. Independents have never done this at volume, and one botched unwind creates a refund violation and a private-plaintiff claim.
solution: Unwind-as-a-service. The dealer forwards the cancellation notice. The desk runs a checklist workflow that notifies the lender, submits cancellations to administrators with the correct pro-rata or full-refund basis, prepares the DMV and tax reversals, calculates the refund and permitted deductions, and produces a compliance file that meets the two-year retention rule. A delivery-day photo and video capture link is bundled, because permitted deductions depend on condition documentation. After 6 months of volume, the desk holds the only dataset on return rates, timing and loss per return in a mandatory-return regime. That data is enough to price a per-unit return-risk cover (roughly $60 to $120 per used unit) through a licensed MGA or insurer partner.
why_now: The law takes effect Oct 1, 2026, so the first returns arrive within days. No US state has had a mandatory 3-day return on used cars at this scale. The 2025 to 2026 run of subprime stress, roughly 30% of trade-ins underwater and repossessions at about 3M a year, means many buyers will discover mid-week that they can't afford the payment. That is the buyer most likely to use the cancellation right.
revenue_model: Flat fee per processed return ($195 to $250). Standby retainer of about $99 per month per store for priority handling. Phase 2: 10 to 20% of premium as an MGA on the return-risk pool. Phase 3: license the cancellation-cascade workflow to DMS and eContract vendors.
non_obvious_insight: Nobody knows the real return rate. Everyone models it on Carvana's 7-day return, but the buyers who return are not typical, because the F&I office sees payment shock and buyer's remorse first. A 48-hour refund deadline is shorter than the time a lender, administrator or DMV normally takes to process anything, so the dealer's exposure is process failure, not vehicle depreciation. Whoever owns the process owns the data, and the data is what makes the insurance product priceable.
first_30_days: Write the cascade checklist by state and by lender for the 20 most common California indirect lenders and 15 administrators. Approach the California Independent Automobile Dealers Association and 10 high-volume independents. Sell a $99 per month standby plan with a guaranteed 24-hour turnaround per return. Handle the first 20 returns manually with a shared spreadsheet and e-sign before writing any software. Log every step's time and dollar cost, since that log becomes the actuarial dataset.

title: 1098-VLI Reporting for Small Auto Lenders
one_liner: Turn a loan tape into IRS-ready Form 1098-VLI statements, with VIN validation and U.S.-final-assembly flags, for credit unions, community banks and buy-here-pay-here dealers that cannot wait for their core vendor.
customer: Credit unions, community banks, CDFIs, independent auto finance companies, buy-here-pay-here dealers and their loan servicers. Any trade or business receiving $600 or more in interest on a qualifying vehicle loan must report, and the statute has no small-lender exemption. The lender pays per form and per VIN cleanse.
problem: Treasury's final regulations under IRC 6050AA (published Sept 8, 2026; effective Nov 9, 2026) require Form 1098-VLI showing borrower TIN, interest received, opening principal, origination date and the vehicle's year, make, model and VIN. Statements are due to borrowers by Jan 31 and to the IRS by Feb 28 (Mar 31 if e-filed), with penalties under 6721 and 6722. Transition relief covered 2025, so the 2026 tax year is the first full-form season. The preamble concedes lenders 'may need to collect additional information' and 'may experience difficulties accurately reporting the VIN'. Treasury declined to make lenders verify U.S. assembly, allowing reliance on the VIN plant code or the manufacturer's final-assembly label.
solution: The lender uploads a CSV from its core or loan origination system. The service validates VIN check digits, decodes them through NHTSA's free decoder, and maps plant-of-manufacture codes through a curated plant-to-final-assembly table it maintains. It screens for new versus used, personal use and origination date, and checks TIN completeness. It produces an exception queue (missing or wrong VINs) with borrower outreach templates. It then generates and delivers the 1098-VLI statements and e-files with the IRS. A white-label web widget for lender sites answers 'is my loan deduction-eligible?'
why_now: The regs were finalized Sept 8, 2026 and take effect Nov 9. Statements are due Jan 31, 2027, giving four months. Big core processors will serve their largest clients first, and 2026 is the first year without a simple summary-statement safe harbor. The consumer deduction (up to $10,000 of interest on new, U.S.-assembled vehicles under the 2025 tax law) means borrowers will call their lenders asking whether their car qualifies.
revenue_model: $2-4 per form with a $1,500 annual minimum. $0.25 per loan for VIN cleansing and exception handling. Enterprise license for servicers and core-vendor partners. Consumer eligibility widget with lead-gen to tax preparers or refinance offers.
non_obvious_insight: Treasury turned a bright-line rule into a data-quality problem and pushed the risk to the lender. Whether a car is American-assembled is answered by plant-code tables and labels, not by anything in a lender's servicing system, and the preamble openly warns of VIN reporting difficulties. The moat is a curated plant-to-final-assembly table plus an exceptions workflow, which the big vendors will treat as an edge case for small clients. Source: https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/09/08/2026-18219/car-loan-interest-deduction (final regs on 6050AA reporting, Form 1098-VLI, the $600 threshold, no small-lender exemption, and the VIN and plant-of-manufacture provisions).
first_30_days: Build the VIN pipeline on NHTSA's free decoder and validate it on 1,000 real VINs. Offer 30 credit unions a free VIN readiness audit on a 500-loan sample tape and show them their error rate. Publish a plant-code explainer for CU and community bank newsletters. Sign three design partners through state credit union leagues and CUSOs, with a goal of $10k in prepaid annual minimums by December.

title: Refundable Deposits Against AI Submission Floods
one_liner: A gateway that makes AI-generated reports, applications and pitches post a small refundable stake, so maintainers only read submissions someone bet on.
customer: Open-source maintainers and foundations, bug-bounty program owners, and other inboxes overwhelmed by AI-generated submissions (journals, grant makers, VC and press inboxes, public-comment portals). Start with OSS security teams and mid-size bounty programs.
problem: curl scrapped its bug bounty in January 2026 after valid reports fell below 5%, and its maintainer floated an entrance fee. HackerOne reportedly paused its Internet Bug Bounty in March after a 76% year-on-year jump in submissions, and other projects have retired bounties. Agents removed the effort-based backpressure open-source governance relied on. Content classifiers lose the arms race to models that write plausible reports.
solution: A stake API and form: the submitter (human or agent) posts a refundable deposit of $5-$50 by card or machine payment. Triage marks the report valid (refund plus any bounty) or invalid (deposit goes to maintainers or charity). Integrations for GitHub Security Advisories, email intake and bounty-platform webhooks. Reporters with track records get deposit discounts, and unpaid stakes flow to the program.
why_now: The curl and HackerOne events are recent and public. Machine Payments Protocol (March 2026) and card rails make small, programmatic deposits practical, and agents now file at scale.
revenue_model: 10-15% of forfeited deposits plus $99-$499/month per program for triage tooling, with sponsor-funded tiers for open-source projects.
non_obvious_insight: Price is the only filter that scales with attacker capacity. An agent must risk money on every claim, honest reporters get refunded, so the cost lands only on slop. Postage as a spam filter failed when senders were humans, but agent-operated senders have budgets and ROI math.
first_30_days: Build a GitHub Security Advisory plus web-form integration in two weeks. Recruit 5 OSS projects that have publicly complained and run a 30-day pilot measuring valid-report rate. Then approach bounty platforms with the data.

title: Kitchen Circuit Retrofit for India's Induction Switch
one_liner: Induction demand is real but low-income wiring cannot handle it, so sell the safe electrical retrofit and finance it.
customer: Lower-income urban households and resident welfare associations, reached through local electricians and hardware shops; discoms and state schemes can co-fund.
problem: After the LPG shortage, induction cooktop demand jumped 20-25x, the government is handing out 500k stoves, and the shift could add up to 27 GW. The Hindu reports low-income uptake is sluggish because of old wiring, overloaded meters and no financing.
solution: A pre-certified plug-and-play kit: dedicated 16A circuit, MCB/RCCB, heavy-duty socket and load-limiting smart plug, installed in two hours and paid in 12 EMIs. The wedge is 500 homes in one city through about 30 electricians.
why_now: The Hormuz energy shock created panic demand in March 2026, and the grid and household wiring are the binding constraint.
revenue_model: Rs 2,500-4,000 per kit and install at about 30% margin, plus an EMI spread and programme fees from discoms.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone counts stoves sold. The bottleneck is the last 15 metres of copper, and the first fire wave will turn certified retrofits into a regulated must-buy.
first_30_days: Design the kit with a licensed electrical engineer and pre-sell it through 20 electricians and one housing association.

title: Tenant Childcare Consortium Powered by 45F Credits
one_liner: Turn a vacant floor in a multi-tenant office or medical office building into a shared licensed childcare center whose seats are bought by 10-40 small tenant employers, each claiming the expanded 45F credit through a landlord-led consortium.
customer: Landlords of class-B office and medical office buildings (setup and management fee), small employers in those buildings (compliance fee and seat purchases), and a specialist childcare operator.
problem: Office vacancy is 17.8% nationally and lenders face $39B of office debt maturing in 12 months, so landlords need sticky tenants. Small employers cannot justify their own center. From 2026 the 45F credit is 40% (50% for small businesses) of qualified childcare spending, capped at $500K ($600K), and the law now lets an intermediary contract with childcare facilities for several employers. Almost no one has built the intermediary. Hospitals, clinics and professional-services firms in medical office buildings have severe shift-worker childcare gaps.
solution: The landlord donates or discounts a vacant suite (ideally lower floors) and a TI allowance. A licensed operator runs the center. The platform acts as the intermediary entity: it signs seat contracts with 10-40 tenants, documents each employer's qualified expenditure for the credit (Form 8882), pools and re-allocates unused seats among tenants, and helps employees route the DCFSA. A third-party operator whose principal business is childcare also sidesteps the 30%-employee-enrollment test that trips up in-house employer centers (to be confirmed with tax counsel).
why_now: The OBBBA expansion took effect for tax years beginning after Dec 31, 2025, so employers are setting 2026 and 2027 budgets now, and the year-end rush to lock 2026 credits is a natural sales moment. Landlords are under maturity-wall pressure and compete on amenities.
revenue_model: Landlord setup fee plus an NOI share of the operating margin (about 10%), a per-employer compliance fee (3-5% of credit value), and operator management fees.
non_obvious_insight: The credit turns a landlord amenity into a purchasing cooperative: alone a 40-person tenant cannot justify a center, but 20 together can, and the credit is richest for exactly the small businesses that fill class-B buildings. A child's seat is also far stickier than free rent as a lease-renewal driver, because losing the lease means losing the seat.
first_30_days: Approach five owners of medical office buildings and suburban office parks with 20%+ vacancy in a high-cost childcare metro. Survey tenants with a two-question form to size seat demand. Line up an operator and a tax counsel opinion memo. Aim to sign 8-10 employer seat contracts before December 2026 so they capture credits for this tax year.
